gen-fs-styro-fs-hoover: Tight, retro, thoroughly bossy. Styro crowds its letters until the counters nearly close, while Hoover, a robust serif with short ascenders, lets each e open wide, good for a couple of lines.
gen-fs-styro-fs-nunito: Nunito reads soft and friendly, with big round bowls and stroke ends that finish away from the stem. And the tension is the draw: Styro's closed, crowded letters against Nunito's open ones, though neither suits long paragraphs.
gen-fs-styro-fs-quicksand: Styro presses its lowercase so tight that the counters nearly shut, a retro, commanding look. Quicksand, a sans of tubular strokes and tall glassy bowls, opens everything Styro closes, which is best for quick lines.
gen-fs-styro-fs-ranade: Styro is retro and commanding, crowding its large lowercase until the counters barely open. And Ranade, a sans with widely spaced letters and a faint watercolor shift in weight, does the breathing Styro cannot.
gen-fs-styro-fs-technor: Technor reads like neon tube, cool and geometric, with one steady line thickness and a wide channel into every bowl. Styro's crowded retro punch is the hook, and best taken in sips.
gen-fs-styro-general-sans: Styro packs its big lowercase so tightly the eyes of its letters almost close, loud and retro. General Sans handles the quiet work, drawing smooth open bends at a steady pressure while Styro takes the commanding lines.
gen-fs-styro-gf-mochiy-pop-one: Mochiy Pop One reads big and round, with a very large lowercase eye and letters hung out like clothespins on a line. Styro's crowded, closed letters make the sharpest difference of all.
gen-fs-styro-gf-prompt: Styro brings retro command, its lowercase large and its letters pressed together until the openings nearly vanish. But Prompt, with oversized small letters and open apertures, feels like a window thrown wide beside it.
gen-fs-styro-instrument-sans: Retro and commanding, Styro crowds its letters until the counters almost close up. Instrument Sans would carry paragraph after paragraph smoothly, its c ends pointing apart like pincers and its strokes never varying.
gen-fs-supreme-fs-erode: Erode is a dignified serif with a tall middle band. Beneath Supreme's understated sans heading, Erode's broad apertures and gentle ebb and flow of weight give the layout an editorial pulse.
